title: How to Turn Team Silo Loyalty Into Stakeholder Commitment 2026
author: Kurt Mueller
source: Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership (kurtmueller.substack.com), September 11,
summary: Mueller addresses a common cross-functional leadership failure: a leader personally repairs a relationship with a stakeholder division, but the team underneath continues treating that division competitively, guarding resources and reinterpreting requests as intrusions. His central reframe is that this is not simply a team attitude problem but a leadership signaling problem -- the leader has not done the work of helping the team see stakeholder success as part of their own success. He offers a short diagnostic checklist (discussing stakeholders only when something has gone wrong, rewarding purely internal metrics, making commitments without explaining why they matter, and accepting 'we did our part' as success) to help leaders see whether they are unintentionally training the silo behavior they're frustrated by. The concrete fix is a ten-minute 'Simple Team Skill Builder' exercise built around four questions about one cross-functional deliverable -- who actually depends on it, what they're really trying to accomplish, what a successful handoff looks like from their side, and how the team will know it helped them succeed -- paired with actively recognizing team members who anticipate stakeholder needs.
points: Mueller reframes persistent team silo behavior as a leadership signaling problem rather than a team attitude problem: teams silo when leaders reward only internal metrics and discuss stakeholders mainly when something goes wrong.
He offers a four-item self-diagnostic for leaders, including whether 'we did our part' has become an acceptable internal definition of success.
The concrete intervention is a ten-minute, four-question team exercise applied to one real cross-functional deliverable, naming the actual stakeholder rather than their department.
He distinguishes 'completed' from 'useful' as the exercise's key discovery point -- many teams find their deliverable technically meets the request without solving the stakeholder's actual problem.
quotes: You finally get agreement from an important stakeholder about what needs to happen. Then your team goes back to work—and almost immediately the old behaviors return. "They're asking for too much." "That's their problem." "We already gave them what they requested.
The more useful question I asked him to consider: "What had he done to help his team see stakeholder success as part of their own success?" This is a different leadership challenge.
If several of those boxes are checked, your team may simply be responding to the signals you are giving them. People pay attention to what their leader discusses, measures, recognizes, and rewards.
What does a successful handoff look like from their perspective? This is where many teams discover that "completed" and "useful" are not always the same thing.

It happens when you consistently help people connect their work → the stakeholder's success → the organization's result. That is how stakeholder thinking gradually becomes part of how the team defines a job well done.
